grade.first_issue: The proposed lower-bound strategy already fails for \(n=2\): from pieces \(3/5,1/5,1/5\), Xiang can bisect the \(3/5\) piece, producing \(3/10,3/10,1/5,1/5\), so Liu receives only \(1/2<3/5\).
grade.summary: The claimed value \((n+1)/(2n+1)\) is incorrect; the actual value is \(2^n/(2^{n+1}-1)\). Although the submission correctly identifies the alternating-rank payoff and proves the basic \(1/2\) bound, both decisive bounds fail.
strengths: Correctly models optimal piece selection via the odd-ranked lengths and introduces the corresponding alternating discrepancy.
Establishes the universal elementary lower bound \(S_L\ge 1/2\).

errors.description: The lower-bound assertion that equalizing all pieces is Xiang’s best response is unsupported and false, as the \(n=2\) counterexample shows.

In upper-bound Case 2, \(x_{n+1}=2L_{(1)}-1+n\epsilon\) need not be positive; for equal initial pieces and \(n\ge2\), it is negative for sufficiently small \(\epsilon\), so the proposed cuts may be impossible.
The upper-bound argument assumes Liu creates exactly \(n+1\) pieces and does not address his permitted use of fewer marks.
In Case 1, the uncut smallest piece need not be last after sorting, so the asserted rank-by-rank ordering is not generally valid, even though a cancellation argument could repair that local point.
